notes: \cpara{Sets the occasion. The author read about the first half of Adam Frank's \textsc{The Constant Fire} before a video dialogue with Frank, and names the experience at issue: a shuttle launch, the stars, a birth. The post dates from March 2009; the book places it among posts of March 2008.}

\cpara{States Frank's thesis, and the rival view the post will defend: a human quality that religion corrupts. The summary of Frank agrees with the publisher's description of the book, which says Frank finds science and religion's ``commonality as sacred pursuits.''}
\cpara{Introduces the post's one quotation, which reaches the author through Frank's book.}

\cpara{The words match James's Lecture II apart from punctuation. The ellipsis drops ``therefore, as I now ask you arbitrarily to take it''. James offers the definition as a working limit for lectures in which he will ``ignore the institutional branch entirely'' and study ``personal religion pure and simple.''}

\cpara{Gives the theme of privacy in the author's words. The only words the post quotes from Frank are ``unique experience of the sacred,'' in the next paragraph; I could not check them, or the passages summarized here, against the book.}

\cpara{Tests several senses of ``private'' with questions: not shared with others watching, different from their experience, unique, or merely hard to put into words. The last is met with sneezing: in that sense sacredness is no more private than anything else.}

\cpara{Gives the diagnosis: calling an experience private shields it from criticism. The post presents this as what it was ``looking at'' in Frank's book, but quotes no passage in which Frank or James uses privacy against a critic. The line of defense in quotation marks is the author's own.}

\cpara{In James's lecture the contrast is between personal religion and churches. He calls personal religion ``the primordial thing'' because the founders of churches ``owed their power originally to the fact of their direct personal communion with the divine.'' So ``the core of religious experience'' fits James; ``as if loneliness were a good thing'' reads a claim about where religion begins as praise of being alone.}

\cpara{Introduces five habits, each explained the same way: something that once shielded religion's beliefs from criticism became attached to the sacred. For each habit the post names a cost, and the costs are arguments against the habits themselves. The claim about their origin is supported by one historical sequence, under ``Faith.''}
\cpara{First habit, mysteriousness. Knowing what the stars are adds to wonder; ``It is a sacred mystery!'' is a refuge from questions such as why God does not heal amputees.}

\cpara{Second habit, faith. The paragraph repeats, nearly word for word, a passage of the author's ``Religion's Claim to be Non-Disprovable'' (2007): the searchers for Noah's Ark, then Bartley's ``retreat to commitment,'' glossed ``I believe because I believe.'' The notes on that post discuss Bartley's term, which named an argument and not only a refusal.}
\cpara{Third habit, the retreat to pure experience: valuing the feeling whether or not its object exists. Its cost is shown with the shuttle launch.}
\cpara{Fourth habit, separation: if the sacred is set apart from evidence, human works such as the shuttle seem unfit to be sacred.}

\cfact{Keats wrote ``In the dull catalogue of common things'' (\textsc{Lamia}, 1820, Part II), and ``Joy in the Merely Real,'' the post linked in this sentence, quotes it so. ``Mundane,'' the word of this post's title, is not in the line; the sense is close.}
\cpara{Fifth habit, privacy, argued earlier with Frank and James.}

\cpara{Concludes that religion should not be salvaged, even as ``spirituality,'' because what is left without churches, scriptures and factual mistakes is the five habits. The post names no spiritual practice and shows none of them keeping the habits; the one book it discusses, read in part, is faulted only for its stress on privacy.}
\cpara{Gives the reason: the habits ``evolved to defend'' the original lie. Religion is a poisoned cup, and spirituality the same cup with the pellet removed and the poison still dissolved in it.}

\cpara{Recommends, with ``I think,'' starting over from scratch. This agrees with the author's ``The Genetic Fallacy'' (2008): ``Clearing your mind is a powerful heuristic'' when a source falls under suspicion. That post also sets a limit on ideas that grew from such a source: ``You are not licensed to reject them outright as conclusions, because reversed stupidity is not intelligence.'' The costs named for each habit are reasons of the right kind; they show the habits harmful, not that every form of spirituality has them.}
\cpara{Draws the contrast: wonder at the stars survives admitting that one was entirely wrong, but a religion that admits it was entirely wrong ceases to be that religion.}

\cpara{Ends with the sacred as the author would have it, answering each habit in turn: believable without strain (faith), there in the world (experientialism), knowable (mysteriousness), shared (privacy), made of the same fabric as everything else (separation).}
